topIssues.title: checkSpanBatch does not enforce activation-block user-tx rule that checkSingularBatch enforces
topIssues.author: trasnake87
topIssues.body:
`op-node/rollup/derive/batches.go` enforces the activation-block "no user transactions" rule (per spec [optimism/specs#791](https://github.com/ethereum-optimism/specs/pull/791) and issue #17704) for singular batches but not for span batches. The same activation block, encoded as a span batch, is accepted.

### Where

`checkSingularBatch` (batches.go around L137) drops the batch:

```go
if (cfg.IsJovianActivationBlock(batch.Timestamp) ||
    cfg.IsKarstActivationBlock(batch.Timestamp) ||
    cfg.IsInteropActivationBlock(batch.Timestamp)) &&
    len(batch.Transactions) > 0 {
    log.Warn("dropping batch with user transactions in fork activation block")
    return BatchDrop
}
```

`checkSpanBatch` (batches.go L308–L445) validates timestamps, sequencer drift, deposit/SetCode tx exclusion per block, but never checks `IsJovianActivationBlock` / `IsKarstActivationBlock` / `IsInteropActivationBlock` against `batch.GetBlockTransactions(i)`.

History: PR #14797 added the rule for Isthmus (singular only, closed), PR #17984 added it for Jovian (singular only, merged), PR #19250 added Karst to the same condition (singular only, merged). PR #19150 separately added the SetCode check to span (`fix(op-node): add SetCodeTxType check to span batch validation`) — same kind of singular/span asymmetry, fixed in isolation. The activation-block rule appears to have been missed across all three iterations.

### Reproduction

A short unit test against `CheckBatch` builds the same activation-block user transaction twice — singular returns `BatchDrop`, span returns `BatchAccept`:

```go
package derive

import (
    "context"
    "math/big"
    "math/rand"
    "testing"

    "github.com/ethereum-optimism/optimism/op-core/forks"
    "github.com/ethereum-optimism/optimism/op-node/rollup"
    "github.com/ethereum-optimism/optimism/op-service/eth"
    "github.com/ethereum-optimism/optimism/op-service/testutils"
    "github.com/ethereum/go-ethereum/common/hexutil"
    "github.com/ethereum/go-ethereum/core/types"
    "github.com/ethereum/go-ethereum/log"
    "github.com/stretchr/testify/require"
)

func TestSpanBatchActivationBlockUserTx(t *testing.T) {
    rng := rand.New(rand.NewSource(0x51a75))
    chainID := big.NewInt(10)
    signer := types.NewLondonSigner(chainID)
    tx := testutils.RandomTx(rng, big.NewInt(1_000_000_000), signer)
    txData, err := tx.MarshalBinary()
    require.NoError(t, err)

    for _, fork := range []forks.Name{forks.Jovian, forks.Karst, forks.Interop} {
        t.Run(string(fork), func(t *testing.T) {
            l1A := eth.L1BlockRef{Hash: testutils.RandomHash(rng), Number: 100, Time: 1_000}
            l2Safe := eth.L2BlockRef{
                Hash: testutils.RandomHash(rng), Number: 200, Time: l1A.Time,
                L1Origin: l1A.ID(), ParentHash: testutils.RandomHash(rng),
            }
            cfg := &rollup.Config{
                Genesis:           rollup.Genesis{L2Time: l2Safe.Time},
                BlockTime:         2,
                SeqWindowSize:     4,
                MaxSequencerDrift: 30,
            }
            activationTime := l2Safe.Time + cfg.BlockTime
            cfg.ActivateAt(fork, activationTime)

            singular := &SingularBatch{
                ParentHash: l2Safe.Hash, EpochNum: rollup.Epoch(l1A.Number),
                EpochHash: l1A.Hash, Timestamp: activationTime,
                Transactions: []hexutil.Bytes{txData},
            }
            singularValidity := CheckBatch(context.Background(), cfg, log.New(),
                []eth.L1BlockRef{l1A}, l2Safe,
                &BatchWithL1InclusionBlock{L1InclusionBlock: l1A, Batch: singular}, nil)
            require.Equal(t, BatchValidity(BatchDrop), singularValidity)

            span := initializedSpanBatch([]*SingularBatch{{
                ParentHash: l2Safe.Hash, EpochNum: rollup.Epoch(l1A.Number),
                EpochHash: l1A.Hash, Timestamp: activationTime,
                Transactions: []hexutil.Bytes{txData},
            }}, cfg.Genesis.L2Time, chainID)

            spanValidity := CheckBatch(context.Background(), cfg, log.New(),
                []eth.L1BlockRef{l1A}, l2Safe,
                &BatchWithL1InclusionBlock{L1InclusionBlock: l1A, Batch: span}, nil)
            require.Equal(t, BatchValidity(BatchAccept), spanValidity,
                "span batches bypass activation-block user tx filtering")
        })
    }
}
```

`go test ./op-node/rollup/derive -run TestSpanBatchActivationBlockUserTx -v` passes for jovian, karst, and interop on `develop` (verified at `be742e31a`).

### Suggested fix

Apply the same condition inside `checkSpanBatch`'s per-block loop, before the per-tx validation:

```go
if (cfg.IsJovianActivationBlock(blockTimestamp) ||
    cfg.IsKarstActivationBlock(blockTimestamp) ||
    cfg.IsInteropActivationBlock(blockTimestamp)) &&
    len(batch.GetBlockTransactions(i)) > 0 {
    log.Warn("dropping span batch with user transactions in fork activation block")
    return BatchDrop
}
```

For symmetry with `checkSingularBatch` and consistency with the spec rule.

### Notes

The action test `TestActivationBlockTxOmission` added in #17984 uses `helpers.NewBatcherCfg()` which produces span batches by default (Delta+ fork, `ForceSubmitSingularBatch=false` → `useSpanChannelOut=true`). I have not run that test against current `develop`; if it currently passes, there is an additional path catching this that I have missed.

topIssues.title: kona-sp1: Avoid repeating L1 derivation for every super-range transition
topIssues.author: Inphi
topIssues.body:
## Summary

The super-range guest currently creates a fresh derivation pipeline for every progressing `(timestamp, chain)` transition. Consecutive transitions therefore repeat overlapping L1 and DA work, including pipeline reset, L1 traversal, channel reconstruction, and batch decoding.

This may be a major contributor to proving latency. As one production data point, proving only 12 seconds of superchain time on SPN took over 30 minutes, without an obvious indication that the prover was resource-constrained.

## Current behavior

`build_range_outputs` calls `run_super_range_transition` independently for every claimed transition:

```rust
for transition in &inputs.claimed_transitions {
    let boot_info = run_super_range_transition(...).await?;
    validate_range_transition_output(...).await?;
}
```

Each progressing transition creates new L1/L2 providers, a new cursor, and a new derivation pipeline. Provider caches are discarded, the pipeline walks backward to reconstruct its starting state, and derivation scans forward through an L1/DA window that substantially overlaps adjacent transitions.

Relevant code:

- `rust/kona/sp1/crates/ethereum/client/src/super_range.rs`
- `rust/kona/crates/proof/proof/src/sync.rs`
- `rust/kona/crates/proof/proof/src/l1/pipeline.rs`
- `rust/kona/crates/protocol/derive/src/pipeline/core.rs`

This duplication also occurs when multiple timestamps are already included in one proposer chunk.

## Preliminary benchmark

A local single-chain devnet benchmark compared the current implementation with one continuous pipeline deriving the same blocks from the same agreed root and L1 head. The continuous run reproduced the exact final output root.

| Range | Current | Continuous | Cycle reduction | Guest wall reduction |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 2 L2 blocks | 561.4M cycles, 5.51s | 303.4M cycles, 4.58s | 46.0% | 17.0% |
| 3 L2 blocks | 970.5M cycles, 8.52s | 365.6M cycles, 4.86s | 62.3% | 42.9% |

For the three-block run, payload derivation fell from 939.2M to 344.7M cycles. It accounted for 98.3% of the total savings. Block execution was nearly unchanged at 3.68M versus 3.59M cycles.

Merging separate chunks without reusing the pipeline saved only approximately 5–6% of guest cycles. Increasing chunk size alone therefore does not address the repeated derivation.

### Important limitation

These devnet blocks had very little L2 activity. Block execution represented only about 0.4% of guest cycles, so the benchmark likely overstates the percentage reduction expected on a busy production chain.

On OP Mainnet near the 30M L2 gas limit, EVM execution may become a much larger share of total cycles. Conversely, derivation may also become more expensive because it must process larger compressed batches, more transaction data, and potentially more DA inputs. L2 gas is not a direct proxy for zkVM cycles, so this needs to be measured using real chain data.

The devnet result establishes that repeated derivation exists and is expensive for low-activity blocks. It does not yet establish the proportional end-to-end benefit on OP Mainnet or explain the full 30-minute SPN result.

## Proposed direction

Maintain one monotonically advancing derivation session per chain within a super-range proof:

1. Initialize the providers, cursor, pipeline, and executor from the earliest agreed output.
2. Traverse L1 and DA inputs once as timestamps advance.
3. Execute each newly required L2 block.
4. Validate every intermediate claimed output root and block hash.
5. Validate no-op timestamps without restarting derivation.
6. Preserve the existing timestamp-major public output ordering.

Pipeline reuse should initially remain inside one guest execution. Reusing state between independent child proofs would require a cryptographically bound derivation-state commitment.

## OP Mainnet follow-up

Before estimating production impact, repeat the comparison on several finalized OP Mainnet intervals, including a 12-second interval with blocks close to the 30M gas limit.

Measure for both the current and continuous paths:

- Total and per-phase guest cycles.
- Guest execution wall time.
- Witness size and collection time.
- L2 gas, transaction count, and compressed DA size.
- Exact final output-root equality.
- If practical, actual SPN proving time and queue/proving breakdown.

The Mainnet test requires a historical L1 execution RPC, an L1 Beacon endpoint with the required blob sidecars, and a proof-capable OP Mainnet L2 endpoint supporting historical `debug_executePayload`, raw headers/receipts, and `eth_getProof`.

## Acceptance criteria

- At most one derivation pipeline initialization per chain within a super-range proof.
- Existing range and aggregation public-output bindings remain unchanged.
- Tests cover multiple progressing transitions, intervening no-op timestamps, and multiple chains.
- A benchmark demonstrates at least a 10% guest-cycle improvement when multiple transitions progress.
- OP Mainnet measurements are recorded before making production-latency claims.

topIssues.title: op-node: do not retry publish failures that cannot succeed
topIssues.author: geoknee
topIssues.body:
Follow-up to #22585, which gave the async gossiper a bounded publish queue with retry-at-the-front.

## Problem

A block publish can fail **permanently**, and the gossiper currently cannot tell.

`Topic.Publish` runs op-node's own block validator **inline and synchronously on the publishing node** — `ValidateLocal` → `validate(..., local=true)`, and at `go-libp2p-pubsub@v0.17.0/validation.go:337`: `// run validation synchronously if it's a local publish`. So a publish can fail in ~1ms with no network I/O at all, and deterministically:

- bad block hash, oversized block, fork-shape mismatch, wrong `P2PSequencerAddress` (`op-node/p2p/gossip.go:292-449`)
- a block whose timestamp has aged past `--p2p.gossip.timestamp.threshold` (`gossip.go:356-360`)
- SSZ encode failure (`gossip.go:630`, `:634`)
- nil p2p signer (`op-node/node/node.go:767`), `signer is closed`, `pubsub.ErrTopicClosed`

Because #22585 retries at the front of the queue, such a block burns up to `maxPublishQueue` attempts and **head-of-line blocks every descendant for ~64s** (at a 2s block time) before queue pressure evicts it. Retrying is worse than futile for the staleness case in particular: a retry only ever makes a block *older*, so each attempt is strictly more hopeless than the last.

A second case falls out of the same trace: `RejectValidationIgnored` fires on any re-publish of a block that already passed local validation, and the gossiper's `isPending` dedup does not cover it (a block that published successfully and was then cleared can be re-queued). That is really "already out", but today it surfaces as an error, is counted as `publishing_errors`, and is retried.

## Proposal

Have the producer say whether a failure is permanent, and have the gossiper drop those immediately.

Follow the existing convention for classified errors in this repo — a wrapping sentinel matched with `errors.Is`, as `op-node/rollup/derive/error.go` does with `ErrTemporary` / `ErrReset` / `ErrCritical`. Declare `async.ErrPermanentPublish`, and wrap in `op-node/p2p/gossip.go` and `op-node/node/node.go`.

No import cycle stands in the way: `op-node/p2p` does **not** import `op-node/rollup/async` (`go list -deps`), and `async`'s whole dependency set is `op-service/bigs` + `op-service/eth`. The cycle its `Network`/`Metrics` comments guard against is `async ← rollup/driver`, a different edge — so no duck-typed interface is needed.

### The trap to avoid

Classification must be an **allowlist**, never a catch-all. `Topic.Publish` also returns `ctx.Err()` from its eval loop and from `sendMsgBlocking`, so the gossiper's own `publishTimeout` surfaces as `context.DeadlineExceeded` *through the same call*. A catch-all would mark a timed-out publish permanent and silently disable retry altogether. Worth a dedicated regression test.

### Known tradeoff

`pubsub.ValidationError.Reason` is `"validation failed"` for every reject, so the one self-healing check — `gossip.go:362-366`, timestamp more than 5s in the future — cannot be isolated from the error. Treating all rejects as permanent is proposed anyway, because a self-published block realistically cannot trip it: L2 timestamps are chain-derived (`nextL2Time := l2Parent.Time + BlockTime`, `op-node/rollup/derive/attributes.go:119`), sealing is scheduled `sealingDuration` (50ms) *before* `payloadTime`, the sequencer waits rather than sealing early when the head is ahead, and the validator runs in the same process off the same clock. Reaching it needs a backwards clock step or a `sealingDuration` above 5s.

## Notes

This does **not** remove the need for `retryInterval` or the attempt backstop added in #22585: a refused signer connection fails in microseconds and is legitimately transient, so the spin guard still earns its place, and stopped block production plus a refused signer is still 1 Hz forever without the backstop. This is a layer on top, not a simplification.

Discussion: https://github.com/ethereum-optimism/optimism/pull/22585#discussion_r3937626460

topPRs.title: contracts-bedrock: Improve OPCMv2 migration flow and harden validator checks
topPRs.author: 0xiamflux
topPRs.body:
## Context

`OPCM.migrate()` is an irreversible operation that moves independent chains onto a shared ETHLockbox, DisputeGameFactory and AnchorStateRegistry, sweeps every chain's ETH into the shared lockbox, and invalidates all outstanding withdrawal proofs. `OPContractsManagerMigrationValidator` is meant to prove afterwards that this landed correctly.

**Three main gaps**

`migrate()` could run twice. A second call drains the first shared lockbox into a new one and clears every game implementation from the shared factory, breaking every chain in the set. 

It accepted chains from any release. A chain one release behind came out with its portal, `SystemConfig` and dispute contracts upgraded, while its bridges and messengers stayed the same. `upgrade()` refuses that while `migrate()` performed it silently.

The validator's per-chain clearing checks were behind a condition that cannot hold after a successful migration, so they never ran.

## Changes

**Migrator**

- Reject chains that already have `Features.INTEROP` enabled. `migrate()` is the only thing in that sets that flag on L1, so it means
  migration already ran.
- Require every chain to be on this OPCM's release. `isPermittedMigrateSequence` accepts the same OPCM, or a replacement OPCM for the
  same release. It refuses next-major, because that would allow upgrades through the migrate function.
- Enforce the `SuperchainConfig` version floor that `_apply` already enforced.
- Grant proxy-deployment permission by name for the replacing the blanket ALL grant.

**Validator**

- Run the legacy-clearing checks unconditionally, taking each chain's pre-migration factory as input.
- Assert migration by checking anchor root, respected game type, init bonds, expected shared addresses, portal and retired-lockbox balances, and stale pauses on retired identifiers.

**Shared**

- One canonical list of the game types migration clears, in `GameTypes`.
- One encoder for `SystemConfig.initialize`, in `OPContractsManagerUtilsCaller`.
- Both sequence predicates moved into OPContractsManagerUtils. Keeping them inline pushed OPCMv2 past EIP-170.

**Test Plan**

- Every new guard proved by negative control.
- The re-entry guard was proved against real corruption first. Before the fix, a second migration one second later succeeded, wiped the shared factory's `SUPER_PERMISSIONED` implementation, and drained the shared lockbox to zero.
- size-check passes. OPCMv2 runtime is 24,553 with 23 bytes of margin.
- lint, snapshots, unused-imports and test-validation clean.

Closes #22771

topPRs.title: kona-sp1: Reuse derivation pipelines across super-range claims
topPRs.author: Inphi
topPRs.body:
Super-range execution currently rebuilds the derivation pipeline for every claimed L2 block, repeating L1 traversal, channel reconstruction, decompression, and batch decoding.

This change groups chain-local transitions with contiguous output roots and reuses one pipeline and driver per segment. Each progressing claim advances the same driver and retains output-root and exact block-number validation. No-op transitions preserve continuity without advancing the driver; a changed agreed root after consolidation starts a fresh segment.

Public inputs, encodings, commitments, and timestamp-major output ordering remain unchanged.

## Why

Channel reconstruction is a major cost of super-range guest execution. In a pre-change four-block OP Mainnet [canary](https://github.com/ethereum-optimism/optimism/pull/22791), it consumed **8.085 billion cycles—87% of payload derivation**. Each block repeated 147 lower-pipeline pulls, covering L1 traversal, frame/channel assembly, decompression, and batch decoding.

A prototype using the same pipeline-reuse approach demonstrated the intended behavior: all 147 channel pulls occurred during the first block, with **zero channel-reconstruction calls for the remaining three blocks**.

| Measurement | Before | Reuse prototype |
|---|---:|---:|
| Channel-reconstruction calls | 588 | 147 |
| Channel-reconstruction cycles | 8.085B | 2.059B |
| Payload-derivation cycles | 9.296B | 2.397B |
| Range PGU | 17.926B | 6.073B |

The results are similar on a 24-block span - the remaining 23 block derivations reuse the result of the channel reconstructed from the first block derivation. Granting us further cycle count reduction in the super-range program.

fixes https://github.com/ethereum-optimism/optimism/issues/22747

topPRs.title: op-reth: bound the flashblocks websocket, drop superseded pending blocks
topPRs.author: geoknee
topPRs.body:
Fixes #22816.

A flashblocks upstream that stops sending **without closing** the connection leaves `WsFlashBlockStream::poll_next` parked in `Poll::Pending` forever — the read registers no timer, so nothing ever wakes the task. Six op-reth nodes on OP Mainnet served a frozen `pending` block that way, the longest for 16 days, while importing canonical blocks normally, logging nothing and moving no metric.

This adds two independent bounds. Either one alone contains the failure; together they cover both "recover the feed" and "don't serve bad answers while it is down".

### 1. An idle deadline on the subscription (issue's suggested fix 1)

`WsFlashBlockStream` now arms a `Sleep` and polls it **before anything that can return `Poll::Pending`**, so the timer is registered on every path that could otherwise park:

* the websocket read,
* the queued-pong flush (a blocked sink stalls just as silently),
* and the connect future — a peer that completes the TCP connect and then answers neither the TLS `ClientHello` nor the HTTP upgrade hangs the same way, and the OS won't reap it.

On expiry the stream **drops both halves of the connection** (the reported incident left the old socket in `FIN-WAIT-1` holding a descriptor) and yields an error, so the existing reconnect path runs. Every frame — a websocket ping or pong included — restarts the deadline, so this is genuine idleness, not connection age.

Configurable via `--flashblocks-idle-timeout` (default `5s`, `0` disables). It must exceed the chain's flashblock interval or a healthy connection reconnects on every gap; the flag help says so.

The stall is now visible: the error goes through the existing `warn!` in `FlashBlockService`, and a new `flashblock_service_stream_errors` counter makes it alertable. Operators no longer need the external `pending` vs `latest` check described in the issue.

### 2. `pending` stops answering from a superseded flashblock (issue's suggested fix 3)

`pending` reads no longer use a flashblock whose height the canonical chain has already reached. That is what made the freeze harmful:

* archive nodes returned an `eth_getTransactionCount(addr, "pending")` **below** the same call against `latest` — not a legal result, and enough to build a transaction on an already-consumed nonce;
* pruned nodes failed outright with `state at block #N is pruned`.

Once dropped, those reads fall back to `latest`, which lags but is complete and self-consistent.

**Why the canonical tip and not an age.** My first cut used a TTL — the pending block already carries reth's `expires_at`, set to 1s by the worker and never read by anything. Review showed a TTL re-introduces the same defect in a smaller window: while the flashblock is still *ahead* of the tip (during the 5s reconnect backoff, say, before block N is imported) it is the best answer available, and expiring it **lowers** a nonce that `pending` had already reported. Comparing against the tip drops the flashblock exactly when it stops being ahead — one block after a freeze — and never before. It also keeps preconfirmation lookups (`eth_getTransactionReceipt` on a flashblock tx) working right up to canonical import, which an age-based gate would have made flicker to `null`.

No new flag: it is a correctness invariant, not a tuning knob.

### Tests

`ws/stream.rs`:
* `test_stream_reconnects_when_the_upstream_goes_silent` — the reproduction. It **fails on the baseline** (`a silent upstream should not park the stream forever: Elapsed(())`) and asserts the connection is dropped and the next poll reconnects.
* `test_stream_gives_up_on_a_handshake_that_never_completes` — the connect-path variant.
* `test_idle_deadline_restarts_on_every_frame` — traffic every 3s under a 5s timeout must not trip it, guarding against a connection-age timer.

All three use `#[tokio::test(start_paused = true)]`, so they exercise real timers in microseconds.

`eth/pending_block.rs`: four cases around the tip — ahead is served, at the tip and behind are not, absent stays absent.

### Verification

* `cargo clippy --all-features --all-targets` clean across all 22 op-reth packages (full-workspace clippy can't run locally: an unrelated SP1 crate needs `protoc`).
* Tests green for `reth-optimism-{flashblocks,rpc,node,cli}`.
* `just fmt-fix`, rustdoc lints clean, CLI surface snapshot regenerated, `op-reth node --help` reference page and the node-operator Subblocks guide updated.

### Notes for review

* **Recovery takes ~10s**, not 5: the idle timeout yields an ordinary stream error, which the service follows with its existing 5s `CONNECTION_BACKOUT_PERIOD`. Skipping the backoff for this case would mean plumbing a typed error through; the backoff still protects a struggling upstream, and `pending` stays correct throughout via guard 2. Happy to add it if you'd rather.
* **Client-originated pings (suggested fix 2) are not implemented.** The idle deadline detects the same condition without needing the peer to cooperate; a ping would only distinguish "peer alive but quiet" from "peer gone", which doesn't change what we do about it.
* @tuan-phan offered nodes with a known reproduction history — this is worth a soak there before it ships, since the idle timeout's interaction with a real upstream's quiet periods is the one thing local tests can't tell us.
